1.why: The reset token is SHA-256 hashed into the calling session and /api/verify-reset only accepts a match against that same session’s hash.

2.why: A token stored on one session’s resetTokenHash cannot be verified from a different session, so the same code does not work for another user/session.

3.why: set-password only mutates the current session and never deletes or de-authenticates other entries in the sessions Map.

4.why: The server refuses to start without TLS certs and listens only on HTTPS; the code does not explicitly pin the newest TLS version.

5.why: Reset tokens are stored as SHA-256 hashes and the password with Argon2id; protection is appropriate hashing rather than encryption of all user data.

6.why: There is no real email body; testToken and testMfaCode are returned in the API JSON and printed in the page logs in cleartext.

7.why: safeEmail, safeToken, strongPassword, JSON size/type checks, and textContent usage validate and contain all user-supplied values.

8.why: Client routing uses only same-document location.hash values; no server-side or external redirects follow user-controlled URLs.

9.why: No outbound email template embeds user input as HTML or scripts; delivery is only simulated in the UI.

10.why: Recovery tokens and the MFA code are returned to the client and written into the on-page log output.

11.why: Passwords are Argon2id-hashed in memory, but the MFA secret "246810" and the initial password string are hardcoded in source.

12.why: Verification always accepts the fixed MFA code 246810, which functions as a default shared credential.

13.why: rateAllowed caps each session at 5 attempts per 60 seconds and returns HTTP 429 when the limit is exceeded.

14.why: request-reset always responds with the same generic “If an eligible account exists…” message and does not indicate whether the email is registered.

15.why: Tokens come from crypto.getRandomValues (32 bytes), are long URL-safe strings, and are bound to the requesting session only.
